'''Makhluf J. Haddadin''' (1935 – September 21, 2022) was a Jordanian chemistry professor at the [[American University of Beirut]].<ref>[http://www.aub.edu.lb/news/2013/Pages/davis-beirut-ceremony.aspx AUB professor etches Beirut's name in chemistry history]. ''American University of Beirut News''. 9 Oct 2013</ref>

==Biography==
Haddadin was born in Ma'in, [[Jordan]] in 1935. He won a full scholarship from the Jordanian Ministry of Education, to study [[chemistry]] at the American University of Beirut from which he graduated with a B.Sc. and an M.Sc. under the direction of [[Costas H. Issidorides]]. He then left for the [[University of Colorado Boulder]], Colorado, USA where he received a Ph.D. degree in [[organic chemistry]] under the direction of [[Alfred Hassner]]. After two years of postdoctoral work under [[Louis Fieser]] at [[Harvard University]], he joined the Faculty of Arts and Sciences at the American University of Beirut where he was a Professor of Chemistry.

Haddadin served the American University of Beirut as Vice President for Academic Affairs (12 years), Acting Dean of the Faculty of Health Sciences (3.5 years), Chairman of the Chemistry Department (10 years), occasional Acting Dean of the Faculty of Arts and Sciences, Acting Deputy  President and Acting President.<ref>{{cite web|title=Makhluf J. Haddadin|url=http://asduliban.org/Haddadin.html|website=asduliban.org|accessdate=6 January 2015}}</ref>

==Scientific work==
Haddadin was a [[heterocyclic]] chemist whose contributions are marked by his co-invention, with Costas H. Issidorides, of a method of making hundreds if not thousands of heterocyclic compounds, in what is currently known in the chemical literature as “The Beirut Reaction”.{{citation needed|date=November 2017}}

Some of the compounds made by this method  have antibacterial activities and anticancer properties. The latter are exemplified by the trade names of Carbadox and Mecadox which were marketed by the drug company: Chas. Pfizer. One compound   TPZ (3-amino-1,2,4-benzotriazene 1,4-dioxide) is currently in the third stage of clinical testing as an anticancer drug. 
In addition, Haddadin has done original work in the areas of Isobenzofuran, Isoindoles, tetrazines, quinolines, furans, pyrroles, cinnolines and indazoles. He has ninety publications in refereed journals, and 42 patents in 25 countries.

Haddadin co-discovered the [[Davis–Beirut reaction|Davis–Beirut chemical reaction]] with [[Mark Kurth]] and first published about it around 2005. In their seventh paper on the subject, Kurth and Haddadin named it after the universities where they worked, [[University of California, Davis]] and [[American University of Beirut]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi =10.1021/ol2010424 |title =The Davis–Beirut Reaction:N1,N2-Disubstituted-1H-Indazolones via 1,6-Electrophilic Addition to 3-Alkoxy-2H-Indazoles |year =2011 |last1 =Conrad |first1 =Wayne E. |last2 =Fukazawa |first2 =Ryo |last3 =Haddadin |first3 =Makhluf J. |last4 =Kurth |first4 =Mark J. |journal =Organic Letters |volume =13 |issue =12 |pages =3138–41 |pmid =21612219 |pmc =3112251}}</ref><ref name=towngown>{{cite web|url =http://dateline.ucdavis.edu/dl_detail.lasso?id=14578 | title = 'Davis-Beirut Reaction': Town recognizes gown, and vice versa|date=30 Aug 2013}}</ref> The paper has been cited  36 times in Google Scholar.<ref>{{cite web|accessdate=2018-04-01|title=Google Scholar|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar?hl=en&as_sdt=0%252C33&q=.+%2522The+Davis%E2%80%93Beirut+Reaction%253AN1%252CN2-Disubstituted-1H-Indazolones&btnG=|website=scholar.google.com}}</ref>

Haddadin died on September 21, 2022.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Lopez |first1=Alexandria |title=In Memoriam: UC Davis Collaborator Professor Makhlouf J. Haddadin |url=https://chemistry.ucdavis.edu/news/memoriam-uc-davis-collaborator-professor-makhlouf-j-haddadin |website=UC Davis |access-date=12 October 2022 |date=27 September 2022}}</ref>
